chapter.title: Fetching a page and keeping a copy

cards.body:
What did your rival's pricing page say last Tuesday? Unless someone kept a copy, the answer is usually gone.

In the clipping service, this is where the scissors meet the paper. Each morning the agent downloads each page, keeps only the words, and files the clipping in a folder with **today's date on it**.
cards.simpler: What did your rival's pricing page say last Tuesday? If nobody saved a copy, that answer is usually lost. Think of a clipping service, where someone cuts stories out of the paper each day. This step is the cutting. Every morning the agent downloads each page, keeps just the words, and puts the clipping in a folder marked with **today's date**.

cards.prompt: Your clipping person reads Monday's paper, enjoys the story about your rival, then drops the paper in the bin. On Tuesday you ask: 'What's new since yesterday?' What can they tell you?

options.text: Exactly what changed, because they read Monday's story carefully
Only what Tuesday's paper says. Nothing was kept from Monday, so there's nothing to compare it with.
Nothing at all, because they can't get Tuesday's paper either

whyNot.a: That's reading, not keeping: even a careful read leaves nothing to hold up next to Tuesday's page.
whyNot.c: That's a fetching problem, not a memory problem: Tuesday's paper is right there. Monday's is the one that's missing.

cards.reteach: To answer 'what changed?' you need two things: the page now and the page before. The agent can fetch today's page any time, but yesterday's is gone unless it was saved. The saved copy is your 'before'.

cards.title: Grabbing the words
cards.body:
*Fetching* means your agent asks a website for a page, the same way your browser does when you type in an address. What comes back isn't the polished page you see. It's the raw recipe: *HTML*, which is the text plus tags that tell a browser where the bold words and buttons go.

Your agent doesn't need the buttons. So the next step strips out the tags and keeps the words, like cutting out a story and leaving the ads on the floor.

Then it saves those words to a plain text file. **The file name carries the date**, so each morning adds a new clipping instead of replacing the last one.
cards.simpler: Fetching means your agent asks a website for a page, like your browser does. What comes back is HTML: the words mixed with tags that tell a browser where bold text and buttons go. The agent removes the tags and keeps the words, like cutting out a story and leaving the ads. It saves them to a plain text file. **The file name includes the date**, so each morning adds a new clipping instead of replacing the old one.

cards.title: One clipping, start to finish
cards.body:
Say you watch Pebble, a made-up invoicing app, at pebble.example/pricing. At 7am the agent fetches the page and gets back a long tangle of HTML. Once the tags are stripped, about 40 lines are left: three plan names, three prices and a short FAQ. It saves them as pebble-pricing-2026-10-04.txt.

Tomorrow it does the same and gets pebble-pricing-2026-10-05.txt, **sitting right next to yesterday's**, ready to be compared.
cards.simpler: Say you keep an eye on Pebble, a made-up invoicing app, at pebble.example/pricing. At 7am the agent fetches the page and gets a long mess of HTML. With the tags removed, about 40 lines remain: three plan names, three prices and a short list of common questions. It saves them as pebble-pricing-2026-10-04.txt. Tomorrow it does the same and saves pebble-pricing-2026-10-05.txt, **right next to yesterday's file**, ready to compare.

cards.prompt: You're setting up the save step for a rival's changelog page (the page where they list what they've shipped). Which naming plan lets you answer 'what changed this week?' on Friday?

options.text: Save to changelog.txt every morning, so there's always one tidy file
Save to changelog-2026-10-04.txt, changelog-2026-10-05.txt and so on, one file per day
Skip the file. The AI model will remember what the page said.

whyNot.a: That's tidiness, not memory: each morning's save wipes out yesterday's, so on Friday you have one page and nothing to compare it with.
whyNot.c: That's the reader, not the filing cabinet: each time the agent calls the model, the model starts blank and remembers nothing from earlier runs.

cards.reteach: Think of each file as one day's clipping in a drawer. Reusing one file name every day is like a drawer that holds a single clipping and throws out the old one each time. Putting the date in the name gives every day its own slot.

cards.title: Mostly text. The exceptions.
cards.body:
Most pricing pages and blogs come back with their words right inside the HTML. Easy. But some sites send an almost empty page plus a small program, *JavaScript*, that fills in the words after your browser runs it. A simple fetch doesn't run that program, so it gets the empty frame.

Other times the site blocks you. Or a cookie banner sits where the prices should be.

You'd think a saved file means a saved page. **It only means something got saved.** So the first time you fetch any page, open the file and look for something you know is on it, like a price.
cards.simpler: Most pricing pages and blogs send their words inside the HTML. But some send a nearly empty page plus a program, JavaScript, that fills in the words later. A plain fetch doesn't run that program, so it gets the empty frame. Some sites block you, or a cookie banner covers the prices. **A saved file only means something got saved.** The first time you fetch a page, open it and check for something you know is there, like a price.

cards.body:
Priya sets up five fetches on Sunday night, sees five files appear and goes to bed happy. On Thursday she opens one. Every day's copy says 'Please enable JavaScript to continue.' All week, her agent has carefully clipped the same empty box.

The giveaway is size: a real pricing page saves dozens of lines, and **a file with one or two lines means the page never arrived**.
cards.simpler: Priya sets up five fetches on Sunday night, sees five files appear, and goes to bed happy. On Thursday she opens one. Every day's copy just says 'Please enable JavaScript to continue.' All week her agent has neatly clipped the same empty box. The clue is size. A real pricing page saves dozens of lines, so **a file with one or two lines means the page never arrived**.

cards.prompt: It's day 3. Your folder holds acme-pricing-2026-10-03.txt (52 lines) and acme-pricing-2026-10-04.txt (2 lines, both saying 'Loading...'). What should you do before asking what changed?

options.text: Compare them. The comparison will show Acme deleted 50 lines of pricing.
Treat today's file as a failed fetch, and open the page to see why
Delete yesterday's file, since today's is newer

whyNot.a: That's a broken clipping, not a real change: Acme didn't delete its prices. Your fetch just got the empty frame.
whyNot.c: That's tidying, not keeping: yesterday's copy is the only good 'before' you have.

cards.reteach: A clipping is only useful if the story is actually on it. When 2 lines of 'Loading...' show up where 52 lines used to be, the fetch almost always failed and the page didn't change. Check the file before you trust any comparison.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Every day the agent downloads each page, keeps only the words and saves them in a file with the date in its name. Open the first file yourself, because **a saved file only proves something arrived**, not that the page did.

Tomorrow: laying two days' clippings side by side to find the lines that moved.
cards.simpler: Every day the agent downloads each page, keeps only the words, and saves them in a file with the date in its name. Open the first file yourself, because **a saved file only proves something arrived**, not that the real page did. Tomorrow you'll put two days' clippings side by side to spot the lines that changed.

cards.body: Open one rival's pricing page in your browser. Press Cmd+A (Ctrl+A on Windows) to select everything, copy it, and paste it into a text file named with today's date. That's a clipping, made by hand.
cards.simpler: Open one rival's pricing page in your browser. Press Cmd+A (Ctrl+A on Windows) to select everything on the page. Copy it, then paste it into a plain text file and name the file with today's date. **That's a clipping, made by hand.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now fetch one competitor page, save its words to a file named with today's date, and check that the file really holds the page.
